Approach

How I design.

Tell a story.

Design should take people somewhere. Every screen sets up the next one, so they want to keep going.

See it in A Family of Buttons

Less is more.

People get bored fast. I cut anything that isn't needed and leave room to breathe. Japanese design has a word for that empty space: ma (間).

See it in my sketches

Make them go wow.

Simple isn't the same as boring. I look for one unusual idea that hooks people and makes them stop scrolling.

See it in Voice control for Blender

How I work.

  1. Sketch ten ideas
  2. Pick one
  3. Push it through versions
  4. Build it

Group Project 2

Voice control for Blender.

Speak, and the model changes. A Blender add-on and a web page that let a 3D expert teach a beginner live, using their voice.

The brief
Help a 3D software expert share their skills with a beginner, live and remotely, using the body for input and output. Video calls and screen sharing were discouraged as the main idea.
My part
The first concept and mockups, directing the prototype build, testing, the demo video and the write-up.
Built with
A Blender add-on, a web page and the browser's speech-to-text.

How it works. From voice to model.

1

Speak.

The expert presses Start and says a command, like “cube bigger” or “add a red sphere”.

2

Turn it into text.

The browser turns the speech into text.

3

Match it and act.

The add-on matches the text to a fixed set of commands and runs it in Blender.

Commands use everyday words. “It” means the last object mentioned, and one sentence can hold several actions.

Three ideas. One kept a person in the loop.

Dropped

AI hover assistant

My idea, inspired by heyclicky.

Point at something and an AI explains it.

The expert would be an AI, not a person.

Dropped

Shared screen control

Annas's idea.

Both people control the same project.

It gets chaotic while teaching.

Chosen

Voice commands

Our pick.

The expert speaks, and Blender does it.

The expert stays in the loop and uses their voice instead of the mouse. The beginner sees the change happen.

Two modes. One to show, one to teach.

Mode 1

Blender does it.

The spoken command changes the model straight away.

“cube move up” Moved Cube up 1 m

Mode 2

Learner does it.

Nothing changes. Blender shows the instruction and the exact keys, and the beginner does it themselves.

GthenZtype1Enter

Why it changed

The beginner watched the model change. But never learned how.

In the first version, the expert's voice did everything. So we added Learner does it: Blender shows the steps, and the beginner does the action themselves. The idea for that mode came from Claude. Our team adopted it and designed how it works.

Testing. What broke, and what we changed.

Wrong microphone.

“Listening” showed, but nothing was heard. I traced it to the wrong mic input on my Mac. Checking the mic is now step one in our run instructions.

Merged commands.

Speaking too fast merged two commands into one. Now users pause between commands.

Objects that aren't there.

Asking to delete a pyramid that isn't in the scene now gets a polite refusal, instead of acting on the wrong object.

Known limits

  • The expert and the learner ran on one computer to simulate the remote setup.
  • English only.
  • A fixed set of commands.

My part.

  • Came up with the AI hover idea and made the early mockups for it and for the voice idea.
  • Directed the build of the prototype.
  • Tested it on my Mac and traced the “hears nothing” bug to the wrong microphone input.
  • Recorded the “Blender does it” part of the demo video.
  • Wrote the prototype and testing sections of our write-up, and the idea comparison.

What I learned

A working prototype showed a flaw the idea never did: the beginner wasn't learning. And the smallest problem, the wrong microphone, was the one that stopped everything.

Next projectA Family of Buttons

Group Project 1

A Family of Buttons.

Four people. Four buttons. Using them shows how our team is alike and how we're different.

Open the team app Open my page
The brief
Build a web app with exactly one button per team member. Each button shows that person's personality.
Team
Annas, Hafiz, Mohammed and me.
My part
My button and personal page. I also put the app on GitHub Pages.
Built with
HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

Drag two of us into the box. See what we share.

Shared in the middle, different on the sides. A bar counts both, so you see the balance at a glance.

It works without a mouse. Tab to a button, press Space to add that person to the box, and press Enter to open their page.

Every button opens a personal page that each of us designed on our own.

My button. From sketch to build.

Why it changed

The kick-by-kick reveal didn't make it into the final build. We ran out of time, and the animation looked hard to build. So the idea moved into my page instead, built as one 2400 × 2000 poster that scales to fit the window.

On my page. A person, as data.

Player card.

I rated myself like a video game player: 86 overall, with six stats from creativity to humour.

Matchday heart rate.

My heart rate during a Barça match, from 64 BPM on a normal day to 182 BPM on a late winner.

Shared interests.

Each interest is tagged with the teammates who share it. Football is everyone's. Chess is only mine.

What I learned

Turning a person into data, like stats, a heart-rate line and shared tags, was quicker to read and more fun than a paragraph about them.

Next projectSketching

In-class activities

Ten ideas. Then ten versions of one.

The prompt: a parent at work wants to stay connected with their child at daycare.

Go wide. Ten ways to connect a parent and a child.

I sketched ten different ways, aiming for range over polish. Each panel uses a different channel, from a phone call to a robot the parent controls.

  1. VR headset
  2. Robot the parent controlsPicked
  3. Video call
  4. Telepresence robot on wheels
  5. Earpiece
  6. Baby monitor
  7. Smartwatch
  8. Morse code buzzes
  9. Shouting, if daycare is next door
  10. Phone call

What I learned

The interesting ideas came after the obvious ones. Once the phone and video call were on paper, I had to think harder, and that's where the Morse code buzzes and the robot came from.

Then go deep. Ten versions of the robot.

I took the robot and sketched ten variations. Each one changes a single thing about what it does for the child or the parent.

  1. Head is a video-call screen
  2. Wheels to follow the child
  3. Voice only
  4. Copies the parent's gestures
  5. Plays pre-recorded videos
  6. Camera so the parent can watch
  7. Touch-sensitive, alerts the parent
  8. Plays songs
  9. Makes food for the child
  10. Dances

What I learned

Staying with one idea pushed me into the details. The same robot could be for talking, watching or caring, and each goal leads to a very different product. Some features, like making food, would need safety testing first.
